items.title: Every Sikh gurdwara serves langar — a free meal for all

options.text: A meal sold to support the gurdwara

A free communal meal served to anyone regardless of religion, caste, gender or background — a foundational Sikh practice originated by Guru Nanak and institutionalised by Guru Amar Das (3rd Guru), who required visitors to eat langar before meeting him

items.reveal:
Langar is served in the langar hall of every gurdwara worldwide. All sit on the floor at the same level — explicitly rejecting caste hierarchy. The Golden Temple (Harmandir Sahib, Amritsar) serves around 100,000 meals daily; volunteers prepare and clean.

Guru Amar Das (1479-1574) made eating langar a requirement before meeting him — including for the Mughal Emperor Akbar, who reportedly sat with peasants before being granted an audience.

In the UK, Sikh organisations like Khalsa Aid extend the langar tradition to refugees, food banks and disaster response — in Ukraine, Turkey after the 2023 earthquake, and at UK floods.
items.why: Practice can teach doctrine. Sitting on the floor and eating together puts equality into the body — more direct than verbal teaching.

items.title: Natural Law has primary precepts and secondary rules
items.claim: What are Aquinas's primary precepts of natural law?

options.text: Five primary precepts identified by Aquinas: preservation of life, reproduction, education of offspring, living in society, worship of God — secondary precepts (specific moral rules) are derived by reason
Only one rule — do good and avoid evil

items.reveal:
Aquinas's natural law theory appears in the Summa Theologiae I-II (Questions 90-97). The eternal law is God's plan; natural law is rational creatures' participation in it; human law derives specific rules.

The doctrine of double effect — an action with a foreseen bad consequence can be permissible if the bad effect is not intended, the act itself is not intrinsically wrong, and the good outweighs the bad — is a key application (used in modern bioethics, especially end-of-life care).

Natural law is the basis of Catholic moral teaching on contraception, abortion and end-of-life care. John Finnis and Germain Grisez developed 'New Natural Law' (from 1980).
items.why: Catholic ethics is not arbitrary doctrine — it rests on a developed rational framework. Engaging with natural law requires understanding the structure (primary, secondary, double effect) rather than treating it as a list of forbidden actions.

items.title: Buddhism teaches anatta — no permanent self
items.claim: What is the doctrine of anatta?

options.text: The soul is eternal and unchanging
There is no permanent, unchanging self (atman); what we call 'self' is a constantly changing aggregation of five skandhas (form, feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness)
Only the body is real; the soul is illusion

items.reveal:
Anatta (no-self) is one of the three marks of existence in Buddhism, alongside anicca (impermanence) and dukkha (unsatisfactoriness). The doctrine sharply distinguishes Buddhism from Hinduism's atman/Brahman teaching.

The Anattalakkhana Sutta — the Buddha's second sermon — argues each of the five skandhas is impermanent and not under our control, so cannot be 'self'.

Later Mahayana schools developed the concept further. Yogacara introduced 'alaya-vijnana' (storehouse consciousness); some Pure Land traditions speak of 'Buddha-nature' that complicates the picture without abandoning anatta.
items.why: Anatta is one of the most counter-intuitive religious doctrines. It contradicts both Western theological assumptions about the soul and lived experience of continuity — and is the central philosophical claim of Buddhism.
